Strict parenting, also known as authoritarian parenting, is characterized by high levels of demand but low levels of responsiveness. Permissive parenting, on the other hand, is characterized by low levels of demand but high levels of responsiveness.

Several large-scale studies have suggested that children of authoritarian parents tend to perform better academically, have higher self-discipline, and exhibit fewer problem behaviors compared to their permissive counterparts (Baumrind, 1991). Furthermore, authoritarian parenting has also been linked to lower rates of delinquency and substance use (Maslow, Fichter, & Hetherington, 2005).

However, it's important to note that the picture is not so simple. Extreme forms of strict parenting can lead to negative outcomes, such as anxiety, low self-esteem, and feelings of helplessness (Darling & Steinberg, 1993). In contrast, permissive parenting has been linked to lower self-discipline and academic achievement, as well as an increased likelihood of problem behavior and substance use (Steinberg, 1990).

It seems that the sweet spot is somewhere in the middle, where parents set clear boundaries and offer warmth and support - this style is known as authoritative parenting. Authoritative parents demand a lot but are also very responsive to their children's needs, resulting in children who excel academically, have high self-esteem, and exhibit fewer problem behaviors (Baumrind, 1991).

So, while there is evidence that strict parenting can lead to positive outcomes, it is crucial for parents to ensure they are striking the right balance. Being overly demanding, without providing the necessary warmth and support, can be detrimental to a child's development.
